text: 7. Storage Architecture

This section is the authoritative reference for how CoLab stores and serves binary blobs — file attachments, images, videos, documents, voice messages, voicemails, and meeting recordings. It describes the *actual* implementation as it exists in the codebase, not an aspirational design. Where the recon grounding notes were checked against the real source, the findings are reproduced verbatim and any corrections are called out explicitly.

In one sentence: **CoLab stores blobs in a self-hosted, S3-compatible object store (MinIO), with an automatic MySQL `LONGBLOB` column as a silent fallback, and serves every blob back through the authenticated backend on the same browser origin as the app.** Clients never talk to MinIO directly. There is no encryption-at-rest by default, and optional client-side end-to-end encryption (E2EE) exists but is off by default.

title: Verified, not assumed
text: The storage layer was confirmed by reading backend/app/src/services/storageService.ts, fileService.ts, recordingService.ts, routes/files.ts, config/src/index.ts, frontend/app/src/lib/image.ts and api.ts, plus docker-compose.yml and docker-compose.live.yml. It is MinIO + S3 SDK with a DB-BLOB fallback — NOT local-filesystem storage, and NOT DB-blobs as the primary path.
7.1 Architecture Overview

The storage subsystem has three physical tiers and one logical routing rule. The primary tier is an **S3-compatible object store** — in every CoLab deployment this is a self-hosted **MinIO** container, addressed through the AWS S3 SDK. The fallback tier is the **MySQL `files.data` LONGBLOB column**, used automatically and silently when an object-store write fails. A third, separate path stores **avatars and chat wallpapers as base64 data-URLs directly in MySQL text columns** — these never touch MinIO at all (see 7.9).

The logical routing rule is the **same-origin proxy**: the browser only ever requests `/api/files/:id/download` on the *same origin* that serves the app. Next.js rewrites and/or the deployment's reverse proxy (nginx or Caddy) forward that to the Express backend, which in turn reads from MinIO and pipes the bytes back. The browser is never given a `minio:9000` URL, an S3 hostname, or (in practice) a presigned link. This indirection is deliberate and is what fixed the cross-host "Couldn't load" attachment bug.

text: **Plain-language summary:** think of MinIO as CoLab's private Dropbox warehouse and the backend as the only clerk allowed inside. Users hand files to the clerk and ask the clerk to fetch them back; they never get a key to the warehouse. If the warehouse is locked (MinIO down), the clerk quietly stuffs the file into a filing cabinet in the database instead — and, importantly, *does not tell anyone* that happened. That silent fallback is the single most important operational caveat in this section.
7.2 The Storage Client (storageService.ts)

All object-store access is funnelled through one module: `backend/app/src/services/storageService.ts`. It constructs a single `S3Client` from `@aws-sdk/client-s3` with the following fixed characteristics:

items: **endpoint** = `config.storage.endpoint` (env `S3_ENDPOINT`, default `http://localhost:9000`; `http://minio:9000` inside Docker).
**region** = hardcoded `"us-east-1"`. MinIO ignores region semantics, but the SDK requires a value; it is not configurable.
**forcePathStyle: true** — required for MinIO, which serves buckets as `endpoint/bucket/key` rather than the virtual-host `bucket.endpoint` style AWS uses.
**credentials** = `config.storage.accessKeyId` / `secretAccessKey` (env `S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`).

text: The module exports a small, deliberate surface: `upload`, `download`, `getStream`, `presignedUrl`, `remove`, `ensureBucket`, the `BUCKET` constant, and the raw `s3` client. Two design choices in this file matter operationally:

items.text: **Streaming downloads (`getStream`).** Returns the S3 object's Node `Readable` so the HTTP route can `pipe()` it straight to the response. This avoids buffering an entire (potentially 100 MB) file into Node heap, which would risk OOM under concurrent large downloads. `download()` (the buffering variant) still exists but the hot path uses `getStream`.

**Lazy bucket creation (`ensureBucket`).** At boot the backend calls `ensureBucket()`; it issues a `HeadBucketCommand` and, on failure, a `CreateBucketCommand`. Per project memory, a bucket-check failure at boot is **non-fatal** — the backend logs and continues, so a missing/unreachable MinIO does not block startup.

text: 7.2.1 Bucket and Key Layout

There is exactly one bucket: **`colab-files`** (env `S3_BUCKET`, default `colab-files`). CoLab does not shard across buckets. Within the bucket, keys are namespaced by purpose and date so the object store is browsable and prunable.

Filename sanitization is conservative: `storageKey()` replaces every character outside `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]` with `_` and truncates to 200 characters. This prevents path traversal, header injection via Content-Disposition, and key-collision weirdness from exotic Unicode names. The leading `files/YYYY/MM/DD/<uploaderId>/` prefix gives natural date partitioning and per-user grouping; the 8-character UUID prefix on the filename guarantees uniqueness even when two users upload `report.pdf` on the same day.
7.3 Configuration and Credentials

Storage configuration lives in `config/src/index.ts` under the `config.storage` block. The defaults are intentionally dev-friendly and intentionally weak — they exist so a developer can `docker compose up` and have a working blob store with zero setup.

rows: Internal backend→MinIO address; http://minio:9000 in Docker.
Defined but effectively unused for delivery (see 7.6).

text: In Docker, the S3 credentials are *mirrored from* the MinIO root credentials so there is a single source of truth. In `docker-compose.yml` (dev/base) `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` default to `colabminio`/`colabminio123`; the backend's `S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/`S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` are set from those same variables. In `docker-compose.live.yml` the MinIO defaults are even shorter — `colab`/`colab` — again mirrored into the backend's S3 env.

title: Weak default credentials are NOT enforced
text: MinIO root creds default to colabminio/colabminio123 (base/dev) or colab/colab (live). .env.example ships these literal values, and the only protection is a comment that says 'change for production'. The production boot guard validates the JWT and LiveKit secrets but does NOT hard-fail on default MinIO creds. Operators MUST rotate MINIO_ROOT_USER/PASSWORD (and the mirrored S3_* values) before any real deployment — a leaked default lets an attacker read every stored blob directly.
7.4 Docker Topology

MinIO runs as a dedicated container. The image is pinned to `minio/minio:RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z` (the pin is intentional — a later release removed the admin console that the nginx `/minio` route depends on). The command is `server /data --console-address :9001`. Data persists in the named volume `colab_minio:/data` (named `collab_minio` in the production stack), which survives container rebuilds — losing this volume means losing every attachment that lives in the object store.

rows: Internal-only; reached via S3_ENDPOINT=http://minio:9000; nginx proxies /minio/ for the console.

text: The key topological fact: **in live and production, MinIO has no host-published port.** It is reachable only from inside the compose network via `http://minio:9000`. This is why presigned URLs are unusable for delivery in those deployments (7.6) and why all real traffic goes through the backend proxy. The MinIO admin console (`:9001`) is exposed only through the reverse proxy's `/minio` route for operators, never for serving user blobs.
7.5 Upload Flow

Uploads are deliberately simple: the client sends **raw file bytes** as the HTTP body (not a multipart form), with all metadata in the query string. The backend buffers the whole body, hands it to the storage client, and records a row. The notable client-side detail is that the upload uses `XMLHttpRequest` rather than `fetch`, purely so it can report progress.
7.5.1 Client side (lib/api.ts uploadFile)

`api.uploadFile(token, file, conversationId?, onProgress?)` opens an `XMLHttpRequest` to `POST /api/files?name=&mime=&conversationId=`, sets the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and `Content-Type` headers, and sends the raw `File` as the body. When an `onProgress` callback is supplied it subscribes to `xhr.upload.onprogress` and reports `Math.round((e.loaded / e.total) * 100)` whenever the length is computable. The code comment is explicit that the request shape is byte-identical to the previous `fetch` implementation — `onProgress` was added as an optional 4th argument without changing the wire contract — so the upload progress bar in the composer is driven entirely by this XHR, since the Fetch API cannot report upload progress.
7.5.2 Server side (routes/files.ts + fileService.create)

The `POST /api/files` route applies, in order: a **rate limiter** (`uploadLimiter`, 60 uploads per IP per minute) and then `express.raw({ type: "*/*", limit: "100mb" })`. The ordering is intentional and important — the limiter runs *before* `express.raw` so a rate-limited (429) request never buffers a 100 MB body into memory. The route reads `name`/`mime`/`conversationId` from the query, rejects an empty body with 400, calls `fileService.create()`, writes a `file.upload` audit event, and returns 201 with the serialized file.

`fileService.create()` is where the fallback behavior lives. It computes the S3 key, attempts `storage.upload(key, data, mime)`, and on success records `storageKey = key`. On *any* exception it swallows the error and leaves `storageKey = null`. It then writes the `files` row with **exactly one of the two byte locations populated**: `data` is set to the raw buffer only when `storageKey` is null; otherwise `data` is null and `storageKey` holds the object key.

title: The fallback is silent — no alert, no metric
text: If MinIO is down or misconfigured, fileService.create's catch block is empty: the file lands in MySQL's files.data LONGBLOB with zero operator signal. The upload succeeds from the user's perspective. Over time this bloats the MySQL volume, inflates row sizes, and can degrade query performance. Operationally: monitor MinIO health independently, and periodically check for files rows where storage_key IS NULL and data IS NOT NULL — those are fallback writes that should be reconciled back into the object store.
7.6 Download Flow and the Same-Origin Proxy

Downloads invert the upload path. The client requests `GET /api/files/:id/download`; `fileService.getDownload()` first checks permission, then resolves bytes from whichever tier holds them. If `storageKey` is present it returns `{ ...meta, stream }` where `stream` is the S3 `Readable`; the route attaches an `error` handler and `pipe()`s it to the response. If there is no `storageKey` it serves `res.send(f.data)` from the DB BLOB. Either way the route sets `Content-Type` from the stored MIME and `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="..."` (quotes stripped from the name).

text: 7.6.1 Why same-origin matters (the cross-host bug)

In a multi-host deployment, the frontend and backend may be reachable on different hostnames/ports. Earlier, attachment URLs pointed at the backend's host directly, so a browser loading the app from host A would try to fetch an attachment from host B — triggering CORS failures, missing auth context, and the user-visible "Couldn't load" error on images and files. The fix was to make the frontend talk to the backend **on its own origin**: `config.apiBaseUrl` defaults to `''` (empty = same origin), and `frontend/app/next.config.js` rewrites proxy `/api/:path*`, `/socket.io/:path*`, and `/livekit/:path*` to the backend (`BACKEND_INTERNAL_URL`, default `http://backend:4000`).

The net effect: an attachment is always `/api/files/:id/download` on the same origin as the page, and the proxy chain (Next rewrite → nginx/Caddy → backend → MinIO) hides every internal hop. `resolveMediaUrl()` in `lib/image.ts` enforces this — absolute/`data:`/`blob:` URLs pass through unchanged, but a root-relative API path is prefixed with the (usually empty) API origin so it resolves same-origin.

title: Same-origin proxy chain for an attachment

text: 7.6.2 Presigned URLs exist but are bypassed

`storageService.presignedUrl()` (a `GetObject` presign, 3600 s expiry) is real, and it is exposed at `GET /api/files/:id/presigned` via `api.filePresignedUrl`. **However it is effectively dead for delivery.** A presigned URL points at `S3_ENDPOINT`, which in live/production is `http://minio:9000` — an internal address the browser cannot reach (MinIO has no public host port). So real attachment delivery always goes through the proxied `/download` stream, never a presigned link. Treat the presigned endpoint as a latent capability that would only become useful if MinIO were given a browser-reachable public endpoint with proper TLS.
7.7 Security Model (Authorization)

Every file route except the public share-link route sits behind `authMiddleware` (JWT Bearer). Authorization is then resolved per-file by `fileService.permissionFor(fileId, userId)`, which returns an *effective* permission ranked `owner > edit > comment > view`, computed from four sources:

items: **Uploader = owner.** If `meta.uploaderId === userId`, permission is `owner` immediately.
**Direct shares.** `db.fileShares.permissionsFor(fileId, userId)` returns any `view`/`comment`/`edit` grants made to that user; the highest-ranked wins.
**Active share link.** If the file has a `linkPermission`, that permission is folded in (used by the public link path).

**Conversation membership.** If the file is attached to a conversation and the user is a member of it, they get at least `view`. This is what lets every member of a group/channel open images, voice notes, and attachments shared there — without it, recipients got 404.

text: If none of these yield a permission, `getDownload` returns `null` and the route responds **404** (not 403) — CoLab does not reveal that a file exists to someone who cannot access it. Mutating operations are tighter: `share()` requires `owner` or `edit`; `unshare`, `createLink`, `revokeLink`, `remove`, and `setStar` require the caller to be the uploader/owner outright.
7.7.1 Public share links (unauthenticated by design)

`GET /api/files/link/:token` is registered **before** `authMiddleware`. The opaque UUID token *is* the credential — anyone holding the link can download the file with no login. The owner alone can create (`createLink`) or revoke (`revokeLink`) it; the returned path is `/api/files/link/<token>`. Like the authenticated path, link downloads stream from S3 when a `storageKey` is present. This is a deliberate "anyone with the link" feature; operators and users should understand that such links are bearer credentials and should be revoked when no longer needed.

title: Troubleshooting a 404 on a file the user 'should' see
text: A 404 from /download almost always means permissionFor() returned null. Check, in order: (1) is the user actually a member of the conversation the file is attached to (conversationId on the files row)? (2) does a fileShares grant exist for them? (3) for a link, has the token been revoked (share_token nulled)? Because access denial returns 404, not 403, the absence of a permission and a genuinely missing file look identical to the client.
7.8 Encryption Model — At Rest and In Transit
Be precise and honest here, because the answer is mostly "no encryption unless you opt in."

rows: No MinIO server-side encryption (SSE) is configured. Objects sit as plaintext on the colab_minio volume.
Raw bytes in files.data LONGBLOB; no column encryption.
HTTPS only if the TLS front (Caddy, or upstream corporate LB / nginx with X-Forwarded-Proto) terminates TLS. Plain-HTTP deployments are unencrypted.
Internal hop is plain http://minio:9000. App code does not enforce TLS to storage.
Client-side AES-GCM; server stores ciphertext and is blind. Gated by NEXT_PUBLIC_E2EE_ENABLED.

text: 7.8.1 Optional client-side E2EE for files

When E2EE is enabled, an upload can carry an `x-colab-e2ee` (or legacy `x-colab-encryption`) header, parsed by `parseEncryptedMeta()` in the route. The file row then stores `encryption_version` and `ciphertext_meta` (migration 0022). In that mode the bytes written to MinIO are **already client-encrypted ciphertext** — the per-file AES key is ECIES-wrapped to the recipient and the server is blind to the content. On download the route echoes an `X-CoLab-E2EE` header (via `setEncryptedHeader`) so the client knows to decrypt locally. The AES file key is fetched and unwrapped client-side; the server never sees plaintext or the key.

Critically, **E2EE is OFF by default** and, when off, no encryption path runs — files are stored as plaintext objects. E2EE scope is also limited (DM/self-conversation messaging context); it is not a blanket at-rest encryption for the file store. Do not represent CoLab as encrypting files at rest out of the box. It does not.

title: Plaintext at rest + plain internal transit
text: With default settings, a dump of the colab_minio volume (or read access to MinIO with the default creds) exposes every attachment in cleartext, and the backend→MinIO hop is unencrypted HTTP inside the network. For any deployment handling sensitive data, the mitigations are: (1) rotate MinIO creds; (2) terminate TLS at the edge so browser↔server transit is encrypted; (3) consider MinIO SSE or full E2EE for true at-rest protection; (4) restrict network access to the MinIO container.
7.9 Media Types — Images, Videos, Documents, Voice

At the storage layer CoLab is largely **content-type agnostic** — `express.raw({ type: "*/*" })` accepts any MIME, and the stored `mime` is whatever the client declared in the query (`?mime=`) or the request's Content-Type. The MIME drives the response `Content-Type` on download, which is what lets the browser render an image inline, play a video/audio element, or offer a document for download. The differences between media types are mostly in the *path* a blob takes, not in how MinIO stores it.

title: Why avatars take a separate path
text: Avatars and wallpapers are tiny, displayed constantly, and rendered by raw /CSS that cannot attach an Authorization header or follow a presigned URL. Storing them as small base64 data-URLs directly in the DB sidesteps auth-header, presign, and expiry problems entirely — at the cost of a few KB per row. This is a correct trade for ubiquitous tiny media; do NOT route large attachments through this path.
7.10 Meeting Recordings
`recordingService.ts` writes to the same MinIO/S3 store as attachments, but through two distinct paths, only one of which works in current deployments.

items.text: **Server-side egress (PARTIAL).** `start()` uses the LiveKit `EgressClient` to run a room-composite egress that writes an MP4 to `recordings/<meetingId>/...` via `sdk.S3Upload` (same `config.storage` creds, `forcePathStyle: true`). This requires a separate `livekit/egress` worker container sharing Redis with the SFU. It is gated by `egressConfigured()` (`EGRESS_ENABLED` truthy AND a non-default LiveKit API key); when not provisioned, `start()` returns an honest **503** rather than failing cryptically. In current deployments the egress worker is not enabled, so this path is dormant.

**Client-side recording (WORKS without egress).** `uploadClientRecording()` accepts a browser-composited `MediaRecorder` blob (webm or mp4), uploads it to `recordings/<meetingId>/<uuid>.<ext>` via `storage.upload`, and writes a `ready` recording row with `playbackUrl = /api/meetings/:id/recordings/:rid/download`. This needs no egress infrastructure.

text: Either way, playback is **never** a public or presigned URL. `getRecordingDownload()` enforces meeting membership (host or attendee), then streams the stored object back through the authenticated `/download` route so an inline `<video src>` can play it while access is checked on every request. `purgeOlderThan(days)` exists for retention, invoked by a background timer at boot.
7.11 Database Schema for Files

The `files` table (migrations `0008_files.sql` + `0027_files_s3.sql`) is the canonical metadata record. Migration 0027 is the pivot to object storage: it added `storage_key TEXT NULL` and made `data` nullable (`ALTER TABLE files MODIFY COLUMN data LONGBLOB NULL`). The invariant enforced by `fileService.create` is that **exactly one** of `storage_key` / `data` is populated.

text: 7.13 Business Impact and Honest Limitations

**What works well and why it matters to the business:** the same-origin proxy makes attachments load reliably regardless of deployment topology (the difference between a usable chat product and one where images intermittently fail). Streaming downloads keep memory bounded so large files don't crash the backend under load. Membership-based authorization means files shared in a channel are visible to that channel's members with zero extra configuration. The DB-BLOB fallback means an attachment upload never hard-fails just because the object store had a hiccup — availability is preserved.
**The honest limitations, stated plainly:**

items: **The S3-fallback is silent.** A down MinIO degrades into MySQL bloat with no alert (empty catch in fileService.create). This is the top operational risk to monitor.
**Default object-store credentials are weak and unenforced.** colabminio/colabminio123 or colab/colab ship as defaults; the boot guard does not block them.
**No encryption at rest by default.** No MinIO SSE; objects and the BLOB fallback are plaintext unless app-level E2EE (off by default) is enabled.
**Internal transit is plain HTTP.** The backend→MinIO hop is unencrypted; only the edge TLS front protects browser↔server, and only if deployed.
**Presigned URLs are wired but bypassed.** The feature exists yet is unusable for delivery because MinIO is internal-only — every real download goes through the backend proxy.
**Server-side recording (egress) is not enabled** in current deployments; only the client-side MediaRecorder path is live.

title: Production storage hardening checklist
text: Before going to production: (1) rotate MINIO_ROOT_USER/PASSWORD and the mirrored S3_* creds; (2) terminate TLS at the edge (Caddy or upstream LB) so browser↔server is HTTPS; (3) add MinIO health monitoring + an alert on storage_key-null/data-not-null fallback rows; (4) back up the colab_minio volume on the same cadence as the MySQL volume — losing it loses every object-store attachment; (5) decide explicitly whether at-rest encryption (MinIO SSE or app E2EE) is required for your data classification.
